If someone is sneaky, it means they do things in a hidden, quiet, and secretive way — usually because they know that if others noticed what they were doing, those others would disapprove, stop them, or catch them doing something wrong.

A sneaky person doesn't act openly or honestly. Instead, they move quietly, hide their true intentions, or find clever indirect ways to get what they want — all while making sure no one is watching or knows what they're really up to.

"Sneaky" always has two things working together:

  1. Secrecy — the person tries not to be noticed or found out.
  2. A motive to hide — they're doing something that they know others would object to, or they want an unfair advantage without anyone realizing it.

If only one of these is present, the word doesn't quite fit. A spy, for example, works in secrecy — but we'd call their methods sneaky, not simply them being quiet.

"Sneaky" almost always carries a negative meaning. It suggests a lack of honesty and openness. A sneaky person is not the kind who faces things directly — they go around the back, so to speak. We associate sneakiness with untrustworthiness, because you never quite know what a sneaky person is really doing or planning.

Think of it this way: if a friend was being sneaky with you, you'd feel that they were hiding something from you on purpose — and that feels like a kind of small betrayal.
Who and what can be sneaky

The word is flexible. It can describe:

  • A person: "He is a sneaky man — he always finds ways to take credit for other people's work without anyone noticing."
  • Behavior or an action: "Copying your classmate's homework and then erasing your name from the paper is a sneaky thing to do."
  • A thing or situation (used more loosely, often with a touch of wit): "Watch out for sneaky fees when you book a flight online — they add charges at the last step that you didn't expect."

In that last example, the fees aren't literally trying to hide — but we call them sneaky because they're designed so you don't notice them until it's too late. The same logic of "hidden to gain an advantage" applies.

"Sneaky" covers a wide range of behavior — from mildly mischievous to genuinely dishonest. The word itself doesn't tell you exactly how bad the behavior is; context does.

  • A child who quietly sneaks a cookie from the jar when their mother isn't looking is being sneaky — but it's harmless and even a little charming.
  • A business partner who secretly moves company money into their own account is also being sneaky — but this is seriously dishonest and harmful.

Both actions fit the word, but the gravity is totally different. The underlying quality is the same: doing something hidden that others would not approve of.
When "sneaky" has a lighter, playful tone

Sometimes people use "sneaky" with affection or humor, especially toward children or in casual situations. If a parent catches their five-year-old hiding behind the sofa eating chocolate and smiles and says, "You sneaky little thing!" — there's warmth in that, not real anger. The child is being mischievous, not genuinely harmful.

You'll also hear phrases like:

  • "That was a sneaky move!" — said admiringly when someone pulls off a clever, unexpected tactic in a game or competition.
  • "Sneaky good" — an informal expression meaning something is surprisingly better than it looks (e.g., "This cheap restaurant is sneaky good — the food is amazing."). Here, "sneaky" is used playfully to mean that the quality was hiding and you didn't expect it.

These uses are informal and relaxed. In serious or formal contexts, "sneaky" is almost always critical.
How "sneaky" feels compared to similar words

• Secretive just means someone keeps things private. A person can be secretive without any bad intent — maybe they're shy, or planning a surprise party. Sneaky adds the element of wrongdoing or unfair advantage that "secretive" doesn't.
  • Sly is close to sneaky, but sly also suggests cleverness and wit — a sly person is cunning. A sneaky person may not be particularly clever; they're just trying not to get caught.
  • Deceptive focuses on lying or creating false impressions. You can be deceptive loudly and in plain sight (by lying to someone's face). Sneaky specifically involves hiding and operating in the shadows.
  • Underhanded (or backstabbing) describes specifically unfair, dishonest dealings that harm others — it's stronger and more serious than sneaky. Sneaky can describe something as mild as taking a cookie; underhanded typically implies real harm or betrayal.
A few more examples to anchor it

• "I don't trust her — she has sneaky eyes and always seems to be plotting something."
  • "The company used a sneaky tactic: they advertised a low price, but the full cost only appeared on the final checkout page."
  • "The cat was being sneaky, slowly creeping toward the fish bowl when it thought no one was watching."
  • "Don't be sneaky about it — just ask for what you want directly."
Sneaky means quietly and secretly doing something you know others would disapprove of, in a way designed so they don't notice — usually to gain something or avoid getting caught.
